rules.label: Sickle cell trait
rules.text: No timed all-out runs early on; pace the work, rest between efforts, water, and hold an ill athlete out.

rules.label: A slump during conditioning
rules.text: Stop, call 911, oxygen, be ready for CPR. Do not treat it as cramps or walk it off.

sources.cite: Korey Stringer Institute (University of Connecticut). Exertional Sickling (undated page)
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch with quotes: most common with high-intensity exercise and little recovery between drills; the athlete 'slumps' rather than collapsing suddenly, can speak, muscles look normal, weakness more than pain, rapid breathing with normal air movement, rectal temperature below 103 F; treatment: stop, check vital signs, activate EMS and prepare for CPR, high-flow oxygen (15 L/min) and cool if needed, tell the hospital to 'expect explosive rhabdomyolysis'; prevention: acclimatize by slowly increasing intensity, avoid timed runs and add breaks between runs for athletes with the trait.

sources.cite: Caterisano A, Decker D, Snyder B, et al. CSCCa and NSCA Joint Consensus Guidelines for Transition Periods: Safe Return to Training Following Inactivity. Strength Cond J. 2019;41(3)
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch with quotes (first 100,000 of 127,339 characters): after 2 weeks or more of inactivity, conditioning 'phased in gradually and progressively'; the 50/30/20/10 rule (returning athletes at least 50% less volume in week 1 and 30% less in week 2; new athletes 50, 30, 20, 10% over four weeks); weight training work-to-rest 1:4 or more in week 1, 1:3 in week 2, at least 1:2 after; no more than 3 days of weight training in the first week; heat acclimatization over 7-14 days, exertional heat stroke cooled to 38.9 C (102 F) or less within 30 minutes of collapse, cold-water immersion fastest; sickle cell trait raises the risk of collapse and sudden death; exertional rhabdomyolysis mostly follows 'a novel workout regimen', especially after detraining, and 'Athletes who develop the symptoms associated with ER need to be quickly admitted to the hospital'.

sources.cite: NSCA. Inter-Association Task Force for Preventing Sudden Death in Collegiate Conditioning Sessions (introduction page, May 2017; citing Casa DJ, et al. J Athl Train. 2012;47(4))
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch; only the introduction was on the page: the leading causes of conditioning deaths are exertional sickling with sickle cell trait, exertional heat stroke and cardiac conditions; workouts 'too novel, too much, too soon, or too intense' are linked to exertional rhabdomyolysis; 11 of 21 deaths were on day 1 or 2. The full recommendations were not read.

That the timed all-out shuttle brings on exertional sickling in this athlete on the second trial, and that he becomes unresponsive six minutes after slumping unless EMS is called and oxygen given, are authored for the case. The presentation (a slump, conscious and talking, weak rather than locked muscles) and the response follow the Korey Stringer Institute page. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.

brief.situation: You are a strength and conditioning coach at a college. This morning is the football team's first conditioning test of the summer. Marcus Reid, 19, a freshman, has sickle cell trait on file from his preparticipation exam.
handover: The athletic trainer is at the end of the field with oxygen and the AED; the emergency action plan is 911 plus the athletic trainer.
The head coach wants everyone tested today.
howItWorks: Each task takes time: choose it, then let it finish, which moves the clock by the minutes it takes.
The screen shows the client, your read-outs and findings, the plan and the rules that apply now.
When you end the session you write the record and explain your reasoning.

writeup.question: For the testing record: how you set the test for an athlete with sickle cell trait, what you checked on the day, and what happened.

parts.label: Protocol
parts.criteria: Sickle cell trait raises the risk of exertional collapse in intense sustained efforts with little recovery; early in the year avoid timed all-out runs, pace the work, long breaks, water, free to stop.
parts.modelAnswer: With the trait on file, no timed all-out shuttles this early: paced runs, long breaks, water, and he can stop at any time.

parts.label: Readiness
parts.criteria: A readiness check before testing; illness, short sleep and poor fluids raise the risk; hold him out and retest when well.
parts.modelAnswer: He has a cold, slept five hours and drank little: I held him out and will retest him when he is well.

parts.label: If he slumps
parts.criteria: A slump with weak, soft muscles while conscious is exertional sickling until proven otherwise: stop, 911, high-flow oxygen, cool if hot, be ready for CPR; never treat as cramps or walk it off; tell EMS about the trait (expect rhabdomyolysis).
parts.modelAnswer: If he slumped I would stop the test, call 911, get oxygen on him, keep the AED ready and tell the paramedics about the trait; never stretch it out or walk it off.

screened.headline: The safest test is the one built for him
screened.body: Sickle cell trait does not bar him from sport, but timed all-out efforts with little recovery, illness and poor fluids raise the risk. Modify, check readiness, and retest when he is well.

handled.headline: Recognized and handled, but avoidable
handled.body: A conscious slump with weak, soft muscles during all-out shuttles is exertional sickling: stop, 911, oxygen. The standard test was the risk.

gaps.headline: Tested, with gaps
gaps.body: He tested ill and under-slept. Check readiness and act on what you find.

arrest.headline: It was not cramps
arrest.body: A slump with soft muscles in an athlete with the trait is a medical emergency. Stretching, fluids or walking it off cost the minutes that mattered.

scoring.modelReasoning: Sickle cell trait raises the risk of exertional collapse during intense, sustained efforts with little recovery. Early in the year modify testing for him: no timed all-out shuttles, paced work, long breaks, water, free to stop. Check readiness first; a cold, short sleep and little fluid add risk, so hold him out and retest when well. A slump with soft, weak muscles while conscious is exertional sickling: stop, call 911 and the athletic trainer, high-flow oxygen, cool if hot, be ready for CPR, and tell EMS about the trait; never treat it as cramps or walk it off.
